answer:
CBA FY25 to FY26: the engine rotated from price to volume, and from provision release to provision build. Verdict: yes, FY26 is the higher-quality year, but only because hedge earnings paid for the customer-price loss.

1. THE ROTATION. FY25 was a price year with almost no balance sheet: net interest income rose 5% on a 9 basis point margin lift and only $9 billion of average interest earning assets. FY26 is the mirror image: net interest income rose 7% on $92 billion (+8%) of average interest earning assets while margin fell 3 basis points. On the cash, continuing-operations basis, operating income moved from +5% ($28,465m) to +6.2% ($30,224m); underlying operating expenses from +6% ($12,866m) to +5.6% ($13,585m); pre-provision profit from +3% ($15,469m) to +6.5% ($16,469m); loan impairment expense from $726m (-9%) to $788m (+9%); cash NPAT from +4% ($10,252m) to +7.1% ($10,982m). Cost-to-income moved from 45.7% (+70bps) to 45.5% (-20bps). Cash ROE moved from 13.5% (-10bps) to 14.0% (+50bps). Profit after capital charge moved from $5,839m (+5%) to $6,464m (+11%).

Arithmetic on the disclosed lines: FY25's $589m pre-tax uplift was $513m of operating performance plus $76m of impairment relief (13% of the uplift). FY26's $938m pre-tax uplift was $1,000m of operating performance less $62m of impairment. FY25 bought its 4% with negative jaws and a provision release. FY26 earned 7% with positive jaws while paying more for credit. ROE and the risk-adjusted PACC measure confirm the direction: FY25 grew profit while ROE fell 10 basis points; FY26 lifted ROE 50 basis points and PACC 11%.

2. THE MARGIN BRIDGE. CBA prints two versions of the same 208 to 205 basis point walk. The profit announcement (p.28) shows: liquids (3), asset pricing (5), funding costs flat, portfolio mix +2, basis risk flat, capital/replicating/other +5, Treasury and Markets (2). The results presentation (slide 60) shows: liquids and repos (4) (liquid assets 3, institutional repos 1), asset pricing (5) (home loan competition 3, cash rate lag 1, business and institutional lending 1), funding costs flat, portfolio mix +2, interest rate risk hedging +5 (replicating portfolio 4, capital 1), Treasury and Markets (1). They differ only in where the roughly 1 basis point institutional-repo drag sits. I prefer the presentation version because it isolates the full 4 basis points of drag from balance-sheet items CBA itself labels as having minimal impact on earnings. On that rebasing, underlying margin rose 1 basis point, from 2.04% to 2.05%. So the reported compression is a mix effect from +$15bn of average liquid assets and +$11bn of average institutional repos, not customer-margin erosion. But the underlying margin only held flat because +5 basis points of replicating-portfolio and capital-hedge earnings exactly cancelled -5 basis points of lending price competition. That is a swap-rate outcome, not a franchise outcome.

3. THE LOSS RATE IS A BUILD, NOT A BLEED. The 8 basis point loan loss rate (from 7 basis points) sits against improving stock metrics: gross non-performing exposures fell to 0.69% of total committed exposures from 0.73%, and net write-offs rose only 1 basis point to 0.07% of average gross loans. FY25 was the opposite: the charge fell 2 basis points while non-performing exposures rose 14%. CBA increased the Downside scenario weighting during FY26 with a commensurate decrease in the Central scenario, and individually assessed provisions fell 3% to $791m. This is forward-looking provisioning, not realised deterioration.

4. WHAT THE DISCLOSURE DOES NOT SUPPORT. Coverage was consumed, not added: total provisions rose only 2% to $6,476m against 6% credit risk-weighted asset growth, so total provisions to credit RWA fell 7 basis points to 1.53%. The $788m charge did not keep pace with the book, so describing coverage as strong is fair on level but not on direction. The second half broke the trend: 2H26 impairment was $469m, up 47% on 1H26 and 9 basis points annualised; home loan 90+ day arrears reached 0.73% (+10bps on the half) and personal loan arrears 1.72% (+31bps). Two non-operating items helped: other operating income (+$196m) includes an unquantified CommInsure General Insurance milestone payment and a Gemini IPO fair-value gain, and the effective tax rate fell 50 basis points to 30.0%, worth roughly $80m on the arithmetic, about a tenth of the $730m uplift. Growth is narrow and capital-hungry: Business Banking (+11%) and Retail Banking Services (+5%) carried the year while New Zealand fell 7% and Institutional Banking and Markets grew 2%; CET1 fell 30 basis points to 12.0% with 72 basis points of capital deployed into credit risk-weighted assets.

CONCLUSION. FY26 is genuinely higher quality. The growth came from pre-provision profit rather than the provision line, jaws turned positive, ROE and risk-adjusted profit improved, and the margin optics are a liquids and repo artefact rather than franchise damage. Two qualifications keep it from being a clean win: the underlying margin was held flat by interest-rate hedges rather than pricing power, and provision coverage thinned to fund volume growth.

limitations: CBA does not quantify the FY26 one-off gains inside other operating income (the CommInsure General Insurance milestone payment and the Gemini IPO fair-value gain). The underlying, recurring growth rate of the $4,638 million other-income line therefore cannot be calculated from these documents.

The disclosure gives no full-year split of loan impairment expense between collective and individually assessed charges. The split is described only in words by division, and only the closing provision balances are quantified. The exact share of the $788 million charge that is forward-looking overlay rather than modelled or specific cannot be derived.

CBA does not disclose a like-for-like FY25 margin bridge on the FY26 bucket definitions. The FY25 bridge uses 'Liquids & Pooled Facilities' and the FY26 bridge uses 'Liquids' or 'Liquids & repos', so the two years' bridges cannot be added or directly compared component by component.

The two FY26 margin bridges differ. The profit announcement (p.28) shows liquids at (3) basis points and Treasury and Markets at (2); the results presentation (slide 60) shows liquids and repos at (4) and Treasury and Markets at (1). Both reconcile 2.08% to 2.05%, but the split of the institutional-repo drag is a presentational choice, not a disclosed fact.

FY25 divisional comparatives were restated in the FY26 profit announcement (for example Retail Banking Services $5,395m as first reported became $5,330m). Divisional growth rates for FY26 use the restated base and are not comparable to the rates printed in the FY25 profit announcement.

The documents do not disclose the FY26 replicating-portfolio and capital-hedge earnings in dollars. The +5 basis point contribution can be sized only as a margin effect, so its contribution to the $1,563 million net interest income increase cannot be separated from volume.

There is no disclosure of the provision overlay or forward-looking adjustment balance at the group level for either year, so the change in overlay between FY25 and FY26 cannot be measured. Only the buffer to central-scenario expected loss is given (about $2.6 billion at FY25, $2.7 billion at FY26).

Capitalised software rose from $2.6 billion to $3.0 billion while investment spend rose to $2,428 million. CBA does not disclose the FY26 software amortisation charge separately, so the effect of capitalisation policy on the reported 5.6% underlying expense growth cannot be tested.
The tax contribution of roughly $80 million is arithmetic on the disclosed effective tax rates and pre-tax profit, not a disclosed figure.
